This FE shell element model is now adopted to simulate the welding-induced stress and distortions for a 24 m and 32 m diameter tank floors. 2.3.1 Welding Model for the 24 m Diameter Tank Floor The 24 m diameter hot tank floor was modeled as a welding assembly of thin, rectangular 347H stainless steel plates. The shell element model was built and implemented in the Abaqus software. Half of the tank floor was modeled by leveraging the tank's symmetry. Figure 14 presents both the tank floor layout and the dimensions of the rectangular plates used for the assembly. Figure 14. Layout of the hot tank floor used in the 24 m diameter tank floor fabrication model. The previous project report [4] compared two models with different mesh sizes to establish a meshing strategy that balances accuracy with a reasonable element count. The strategy employing a minimum size of 8*20mm2 proved efficient and accurate for the large tank floor models. To maintain a similar calculation time to that of the 39.6 m diameter tank floor, the mesh size and gradient were reduced to adapt to the 24 m tank diameter while keeping a similar calculation time. Figure 15 presents the mesh model, which consists of 76,293 elements and 74,525 nodes. This meshing uses a mixture of four-node linear quadrilateral and three-node linear triangular element types for both heat transfer (defined as DS4/DS3) and non-linear elastic-plastic calculations (S4R/S3R). Although the floor in a shell element model lacks geometric thickness, this parameter is factored in via section integration points. In this case, a shell thickness of 7 mm was used, considering five thickness integration points and employing the Simpson thickness integration rule. Similar to the solid model, this shell element model utilized a Goldak double ellipsoidal heat source with simplified one-pass welding [4,15]. 12 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. The sequentially coupled thermo-elastic-plastic FE method was used, and the welding simulation of tank floor fabrication was performed along the short and long edges of each floor plate. All the short edges were welded at the same time, and then all the long edges were also welded simultaneously to minimize the simulation time, considering that there is no interaction between welding due to the large size plates (see Figure 16).
